Date: 2026-05-01 15:00 PT

Attendees: Ben Foster (Redwood AE), Sara Lin (Redwood SE), Tom Caldwell (Mariner - Head of Platform), Aisha Khan (Mariner - SRE), Luis Ortega (Mariner - CTO, 1st 10 mins)

Notes: Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations and cost model
summary: Redwood ran an Optimize product walkthrough for Mariner Payments covering batching strategies, prefix vs KV caching tradeoffs, and a cost model showing token/unit economics across model variants and quantization. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated; primary constraints are 300 qps peak, 95th p latency target ~150ms for short chat flows, and strict PCI-like data residency and audit log needs. AE & SE agreed to send a detailed cost spreadsheet and schedule a pilot benchmark.
topics: Overview of batching and continuous batching benefits
Prefix cache vs KV cache tradeoffs for conversational sessions
Cost model: tokens saved vs additional memory / GPU cost
Next steps: spreadsheet, pilot benchmarks, security docs
transcript:
[00:00] Ben (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate the time. Quick intro - I'm Ben, AE on this account, Sara is our SE who will run through the optimize walkthrough. Luis will jump in for first few mins.
[00:18] Luis Ortega (Mariner - CTO): Hi all - sorry short day for me, but wanted to hear the cost model bits.
[00:24] Sara (Redwood SE): Cool, thanks. I'll share screen in a sec - we'll do a short agenda: batching basics, prefix vs KV cache, demo of cost spreadsheet, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:40] Tom (Mariner): Sounds good. Our context: roughly 300 qps peak for auth/chat flows, session length median 12 turns, sometimes long 50-100 turn sessions for dispute resolution threads. Latency SLO: 95th around 150-200ms for short flows. We're also considering dedicated for PCI scope reasons.
[01:02] Sara: Great that's helpful. Two quick clarifications - are you mostly doing short prompt completions for UI or are you doing heavy RAG with large context?
[01:12] Aisha: Mostly UI chat and some RAG on customer statements, we'll send sample prompts.
[01:18] Ben: Ok, so first section - batching. High level, continuous batching pools concurrent requests and fills micro-batches to increase GPU utilization, reduces cost per token but can add queueing latency.
[01:35] Sara: Example tradeoff - at 300 qps with 8k context model, moving batch window from 10ms to 30ms increased median latency by ~8ms but increased throughput and reduced per-token GPU time by ~18%.
[01:50] Tom: Is that measured on your hosted fleet or Dedicated?
[01:54] Sara: Those numbers were on Redwood Dedicated with A100-like hardware; hosted numbers are similar but reflect multi-tenant variance. We also show batch-size curves in the spreadsheet.
[02:06] [02:06] Speaker 5: mm-hmm
[02:12] Sara: Next - prefix cache vs KV cache. Quick def: prefix cache stores token-level prefixes per session (cheap for short sessions), KV cache stores transformer KV cache to skip recomputation across longer contexts.
[02:29] Ben: Note, in some docs people call KV "K-V cash" in transcripts lol.
[02:33] Aisha: (laughs) yep we've seen that in our logs.
[02:36] Sara: Practical guidance: for median session lengths under ~20 tokens or turns, prefix caching often gives most wins with minimal memory. For long-running sessions or RAG where you re-query similar long context ranges, KV caching reduces compute by skipping attention recompute.
[02:55] Tom: Memory overhead? Our infra team is sensitive to GPU memory - we run some batch jobs plus inference on same cluster.
[03:04] Sara: KV cache increases memory proportional to sequence length and hidden size. E.g., for a 32k context model with 96 layers, KV can be tens of GBs per session if you store full tokens - so we recommend per-session eviction and sharded KV store, or use compressed/quantized KV profiles.
[03:23] Tom: Ok. Is there an automatic eviction policy in Redwood Private?
[03:27] Sara: Yes, you can set TTLs, LRU and size-based eviction; in Dedicated we usually run per-tenant shards with a TTL of 30-60 minutes for interactive use cases.
[03:39] [03:39] Ben: Slide - cost model. Sara, can you walk through the spreadsheet scenario?
[03:44] Sara: Sure; shared spreadsheet link in chat (redwood.com/optimize/sample-batching-spreadsheet). Scenario A: hosted, base 8k model, no KV cache, default batching -> cost X per 1M tokens. Scenario B: Dedicated, 8k model, continuous batching + prefix cache -> cost Y which is ~25% lower on token compute. Scenario C: Dedicated, 32k model, KV cache for long sessions -> compute cost per token is lower for long sessions but memory/GPU cost increases.
[04:13] Aisha: Do you break out network egress/caching infra costs vs pure token compute?
[04:17] Sara: Yes - spreadsheet has tabs: compute, storage (KV store), network egress, and ops (support). We model amortized GPU cost per hour and spread across tokens served.
[04:27] Tom: How do you account for fallback routing - if dedicated is saturated, you route to hosted lower-spec model? Does the cost model include fallback hit rates?
[04:36] Sara: We include a configurable fallback factor - you can set expected percent of requests that fall back to hosted and the spreadsheet shows blended latency/cost. Important for availability and SLA design.
[04:46] Ben: Customer question - what's the sweet spot for batch size for sub-200ms 95th?
[04:51] Sara: For 8k models, we typically see batch sizes 8-16 with a micro-batching window 15-30ms keep 95th <200ms for single token responds. For multi-token generation you have to account for token-by-token latency, so we show curves.
[05:07] [05:07] Tom: Could you share the curve for 300 qps?
[05:12] Sara: Yes - I'll run a quick estimate. If you have 300 qps with average 2 concurrent tokens per request, you're looking at an effective concurrent requests of ~600. With batching 12 this gives about 50 micro-batches per second - our estimate shows 95th ~120-160ms on Dedicated with optimized kernels. I'll add the chart to the spreadsheet.
[05:34] Aisha: What about quantization - do you recommend 8-bit/fp16? How does quantization affect KV cache behavior?
[05:41] Sara: We support per-model quantization profiles. Int8/4-bit saves memory and increases throughput but can slightly change latency characteristics. For KV caches, quantized KV reduces memory footprint proportionally but you must validate model quality; our Optimize tab recommends which quant profiles matched customer workloads in our internal evals.
[05:59] Tom: Any concerns about quality drift?
[06:02] Ben: We run evals tied to prompt sets and regression alerts; if quantization changes output distribution, we flag and recommend moving to a higher-precision variant.
[06:11] Sara: Quick demo - here's a sample scenario for Mariner: 300 qps, median 12 turns, 50% short sessions, 20% long sessions. Spreadsheet shows net token savings of ~22% using prefix cache + micro-batching and up to 47% saving for long sessions with KV cache. But note the KV memory incremental cost.
[06:35] [06:35] Tom: That saving is token compute only, correct? Does it include storage cost for KV entries?
[06:39] Sara: Correct - the spreadsheet line items show compute savings and then subtract amortized KV store cost; net savings remain positive for workloads with >30% long-session prevalence.
[06:49] Aisha: On Dedicated licensing, what are the commit levels and how do you handle burst?
[06:54] Ben: Dedicated is reserved capacity with optional burst credits; we can model monthly commit scenarios in the spreadsheet. For Mariner we can show 2 flavors: baseline commit for 70% normal plus 30% burst credits.
[07:07] [07:07] Speaker 5: mm
[07:14] Sara: Security notes - Private/Dedicated support VPC, KMS/HSM integration for keys, and audit logs for request-level tracing. We'll attach the SOC2 summary and network architecture doc.
[07:30] Tom: We need per-token audit logs and retention controls, and proof that logs can be kept only in our VPC.
[07:38] Ben: That's supported with Private deployments; for Dedicated we provide a control plane with audit logging export. We'll include specifics in the security pack.
[07:47] Sara: Back to technical - KV sharding. For large numbers of concurrent sessions, we shard KV across nodes and evict by TTL or size; we can pre-warm common prefixes.
[07:59] Tom: Pre-warm how?
[08:01] Sara: You can preload KV for known common flows, e.g., onboarding flows or typical dispute templates. That avoids cold compute on first few tokens.
[08:11] Aisha: Do you have any sample numbers for memory per session for 8k vs 32k?
[08:15] Sara: Quick ballpark: 8k context model KV per session ~0.2-0.5GB depending on hidden size and layers; 32k can be 2-10x that if you store full KVs. We'll include per-model numbers in the spreadsheet tab.
[08:33] Tom: If we compress KV or quantize it, does that impact latency read/write?
[08:38] Sara: Slightly, compression adds CPU overhead on the host side but reduces memory pressure and network egress. Our experiments show net latency impact under 5-10ms for typical setups.
[08:52] Ben: Question from procurement - do you support term-based pricing tied to commits?
[08:56] Sara: Yes; we have monthly/annual reserved capacity contracts for Dedicated and enterprise packages for Private. Ben will follow up with commercial terms.
[09:05] [09:05] Tom: Any other examples like a bank we can reference?
[09:09] Ben: We worked with Aurora Finance (see case study) - similar constraints and we saved ~30% token compute by moving to prefix+KV hybrid and tuning batch windows. We'll share that case study.
[09:20] Aisha: How do we validate quality changes post-quantization? Do you run A/B or shadow testing?
[09:26] Sara: Both. You can do shadow traffic and A/B with rollouts in the Console. Our Rollouts feature supports canary + automatic fallback if quality metrics degrade. We can integrate your QA prompt set to measure BLEU/embedding similarity or custom metrics.
[09:45] [09:45] Tom: Could you also show a short run of the cost model with our numbers?
[09:50] Sara: Yes let me edit the shared sheet live - entering: 300 peak qps, 12 median turns, 50% short, 20% long sessions.
[10:08] Sara: Ok sheet updates - projected monthly tokens 1.6B, compute hours 420h if no batching. With continuous batching and prefix cache projected compute hours 325h. Net monthly cost delta shown in Summary tab.
[10:27] Tom: Those are promising. Where do I see the assumptions for GPU price?
[10:31] Sara: In assumptions tab - we use A100 equivalent $6/hr amortized for Dedicated baseline, hosted blended rate slightly higher. You can edit to your local cloud rates.
[10:41] [10:41] Speaker 5: uh-huh
[10:47] Aisha: For pilot benchmarking, how long and what do you need from us?
[10:51] Ben: 1-2 day pilot - we need a sample prompt set, a traffic replay (or synthetic generator), and an environment endpoint. We'll run a dedicated benchmark and provide latency and token-cost reports.
[11:05] Tom: Who runs the pilot on our infra? Can Redwood run in our VPC?
[11:10] Sara: Yes we offer Private deployment or we can run a short-lived Dedicated pilot in your account with our tooling. For strict PCI concerns, Private is recommended.
[11:20] Aisha: Ok we'll discuss internally.
[11:23] [11:23] Ben: Quick Q&A lightning round -any blockers we should know?
[11:27] Tom: Need to confirm compliance checklist and retention. Also we'll want to see per-token audit and SAML integrations.
[11:34] Ben: We'll send SOC2 and SAML docs and a proposed pilot schedule.
[11:38] Sara: One last technical note - for mixed workloads we recommend hybrid caching: prefix cache for short flows and a small KV store for long sessions; auto-promote sessions to KV if they exceed a threshold. That gives most savings with controlled memory.
[11:55] Tom: Auto-promote. Nice. How threshold set?
[11:58] Sara: Configurable, e.g., 20 turns or N tokens threshold. We can make it adaptive too.
[12:06] [12:06] Ben: Alright wrapping up - recap of next steps in chat, any final questions?
[12:12] Aisha: No final Qs. Looks good, will send traces and prompts.
[12:15] Tom: Thanks Ben and Sara.
[12:18] Ben: Thanks everyone, speak soon.
[12:20] [End of recording]
